lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why freedom comes whole
lead.head: Freedom isn’t sold separately

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 16

body: “Can we grow rich and still beat our wives? Or do we have to stop beat­ing our wives to grow rich?” The ques­tion came from a friend of Amit Varma’s who runs one of Asia’s big­gest busi­nesses, and who let Varma use the ques­tion but not his name. {016-S01}

At heart, Varma said, it asks whether pros­per­ity needs moder­nity: free­dom, con­sent, au­ton­omy. His an­swer is that all kinds of free­dom have to come hand in hand, and that true pros­per­ity, even in the ma­te­rial sense[[x1]], is im­pos­si­ble with­out them. {016-C01}
When Varma first told him the ques­tion, Ajay Shah said at once that it be­longed in their episode on China. What fol­lowed was a his­tory of two great bets against free­dom.
## The Soviet bet

The Soviet Union bet that free­dom mat­tered in no do­main. It forced in­dus­tri­al­i­sa­tion through cen­tral plan­ning and cru­elty, built a nu­clear bomb by 1949, and looked to many like the fu­ture.
Then, in 1989, it col­lapsed under the weight of its own con­tra­dic­tions.
Shah bor­rowed a term from com­puter en­gi­neer­ing: tech­ni­cal debt. “You can ap­pear to make some progress, but your sins are going to catch up with you,” he said. {016-C02}

Behind it all were ideas. “Nothing mat­ters more than ideas,” Shah said, and in every free coun­try a camp of thinkers has ar­gued for less free­dom. They ad­mired the Soviet Union first, and China next.
## The China bet

The Chinese Communist Party stud­ied the Soviet fall and drew a les­son: short­ages kill regimes. So it opened up to con­sumer goods, trade and for­eign in­vest­ment, while keep­ing one-party rule and lim­its on per­sonal free­dom.
For a while it worked. Hundreds of mil­lions of peo­ple came out of poverty, and global firms com­mit­ted them­selves to the China story.

Now, Shah ar­gued, the model is break­ing. He named five forces: Xi Jinping’s re­turn to Maoist and Leninist pol­i­tics, the mis­man­age­ment of COVID, con­fronta­tion with the ad­vanced economies, un­sus­tain­able eco­nomic man­age­ment and a pop­ulist at­tack on the country’s other elites.
“This whole pack­age of griev­ance and anger and na­tion­al­ism is re­ally toxic and the China model is bro­ken and it will not work,” he said. {016-C20}
The regime is in charge and the bor­der is in­tact. But like the Soviet model in 1989, he said, the China model has lost its cred­i­bil­ity.
## Ends and means

Amit Varma re­told the story from Mao on­wards, through Adam Smith’s “man of sys­tem”, the plan­ner in love with his own plan, and through the Leninist ma­chin­ery that still runs be­neath China’s re­forms.

He also pressed the other side. Deng Xiaoping’s China gave a gen­er­a­tion the kind of mo­bil­ity that India, Varma said, still does not see. If Deng’s aim was to lift a few hun­dred mil­lion peo­ple out of poverty, he ar­gued, he suc­ceeded.
Shah replied that great states­men play for 50 and 100 years, and on that mea­sure Taiwan, not China, has got its act to­gether.
“You need to re­ally fix the free­dom side first. You need to get on the jour­ney to a lot more free­dom. Then good things will come,” he said. {016-C19}
He even had a book in mind for Deng: *In Service of the Republic*, which he wrote with Vijay Kelkar. Varma called it the great­est plug he had ever seen any­one give their own book.
On the larger point, there was no quar­rel. “Freedom is ev­ery­thing,” Varma said.

second.label: The Great Leap Forward
second.head: The sparrow’s revenge
second.deck: Amit Varma on Mao’s 1958 campaign and the delusion of the master plan

pic.caption: Four Pests campaign poster, 1958: a sword skewers mosquito, fly, sparrow and rat

body: In 1958, Mao or­dered every spar­row in China killed[[x3]][[x2]]. Farmers were suf­fer­ing be­cause spar­rows ate their grain, and the cam­paign was hailed as a nec­es­sary step by a strong leader. {016-S06}

Countless spar­rows died. But spar­rows ate lo­custs, and once they were gone, lo­custs mul­ti­plied and de­stroyed China’s crops. No fewer than 45 mil­lion peo­ple died in the three years that fol­lowed. {#famine}

Amit Varma read the pas­sage aloud be­fore re­veal­ing its au­thor: him­self, in a 2016 col­umn on de­mon­eti­sa­tion. The spar­row cam­paign, he had writ­ten, was one of many edicts of the Great Leap Forward, all born of the delu­sion that a leader could re­design a whole so­ci­ety to fit a mas­ter plan.

quote.text: Sparrows ate lo­custs. And once the bal­ance in the ecosys­tem changed, lo­custs pro­lif­er­ated and de­stroyed China’s crops.

third.head: Let them eat yogurt

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on four flavours of yogurt

body: When the Soviet Union fell, the Chinese Communist Party stud­ied it in­ten­sively, Ajay Shah said, and swore to do what­ever it took to sur­vive.
It drew a homely les­son. “They un­der­stood that the Soviet Union col­lapsed be­cause they were not able to make more than four kinds of flavoured yo­gurt,” Shah said. {016-S03}

So China opened up to a pri­vate con­sumer econ­omy with 400 kinds of yo­gurt, to trade and to for­eign in­vest­ment. The state stayed on top, with one-party rule and lim­its on per­sonal free­dom. “And by God,” Shah said, “they did ig­nite a growth process.”

It also showed what co­er­cion can co­or­di­nate. China did much the same as India’s UPI, forc­ing ev­ery­one onto one pay­ment stan­dard, and quick, vis­i­ble wins like that per­suaded ad­mir­ers that wise of­fi­cials could guide an econ­omy. {016-C03}

p2.deck: Moscow bet freedom was unnecessary, Beijing that a little would do. Amit Varma says it comes as a package. {016-C01}

quote.text: If we are to pros­per as peo­ple, to grow as in­di­vid­u­als, all kinds of free­dom have to come hand in hand.

box.title: What Xi undid
box.text: Deng Xiaoping built term lim­its, a suc­ces­sion sys­tem and a stance of bid­ing time with the West. Xi Jinping, Ajay Shah said, undid them[[x18]], con­cen­trated power in him­self and his cronies, and fanned na­tion­al­ism among young men. {#termlimits}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: The tycoon’s dinner question
sections.caption: a question of wives and wealth
body: Over din­ner abroad, a friend of Amit Varma’s asked a ques­tion so beau­ti­fully formed that Varma asked if he could quote him. The friend, who runs one of the big­gest busi­nesses in Asia and holds de­grees in phi­los­o­phy and an­thro­pol­ogy, said no to his name but yes to the ques­tion. {016-S01}

Can we grow rich and still beat our wives, or must we stop to grow rich? At heart, Varma said, it is a ques­tion about moder­nity, by which he means clas­si­cal lib­eral val­ues: free­dom, con­sent and au­ton­omy[[x8]].

The me­dian Indian male, he guessed, would an­swer that pros­per­ity and tra­di­tion can come to­gether. Varma’s own po­si­tion, which he called con­tro­ver­sial, is that true pros­per­ity in all its senses, even the ma­te­rial sense, is im­pos­si­ble in the long run with­out moder­nity[[x7]]. {016-C01}
## Two lenses
Ajay Shah sug­gested two ways into the ques­tion. The first is to ask whether the an­swer dif­fers for an in­di­vid­ual, who may get ahead with Neanderthal val­ues, and for a whole so­ci­ety.

The sec­ond is to sup­pose the an­swer is no: that pros­per­ity needs “the full pack­age of en­light­en­ment val­ues”, and the pack­age is not di­vis­i­ble. Some would then make their peace with those val­ues. Others, Shah won­dered, might choose to sac­ri­fice the pros­per­ity. {#sacrifice}
~ Shah had said, when Varma first put the ques­tion to him, that it be­longed in their China episode. The China story, Varma said, is not re­ally about China. “It’s about all of us.”

quote.text: If we are to pros­per as peo­ple, to grow as in­di­vid­u­als, all kinds of free­dom have to come hand in hand.

art.caption: Amit Varma on a question of wives and wealth

sections.label: The first bet
sections.head: Moscow’s sprint, Moscow’s debt
sections.caption: the Soviet backdrop
body: The Soviet Union, Amit Varma said, rested on the claim that free­dom mat­tered in no do­main, per­sonal, eco­nomic or po­lit­i­cal. That was a lie twice over: the pros­per­ity was a lie, and a sys­tem like that had to give.

Varma ex­plained the fall with Timur Kuran’s idea of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion[[x9]]. Under re­pres­sion, every in­di­vid­ual was scared to speak up, so no­body seemed to be against the regime. Once peo­ple saw that oth­ers felt the same, the si­lence be­came a pref­er­ence cas­cade. {016-C06}
Ajay Shah called the regime’s early growth a sprint that ran up tech­ni­cal debt, a phrase from com­puter en­gi­neer­ing. {016-C02}
## A camp that never leaves

The Soviet Union’s dis­as­ters and achieve­ments alike, Shah said, were the work of “an aca­demic scrib­bler called Karl Marx”, who never saw the out­side world be­yond the British Library. {016-J11} In every free coun­try, he added, a camp of thinkers has ar­gued for less free­dom. {016-C04}

Some ar­gued that a poor coun­try should be thug­gish first and add democ­racy later. It was a great de­bate of the Indian free­dom move­ment, Shah said, when fe­male lit­er­acy in 1947 was 6 or 7 per cent. {#literacy}
~ Chile, Taiwan and South Korea made the move from dic­ta­tor­ship, he said, but it is not easy. The Soviet econ­omy was so dis­torted that 1989 burned it to the ground.

quote.text: So in the end, it is all about ideas. Nothing mat­ters more than ideas.

portraits.caption: Karl Marx
portraits.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain

sections.label: The second bet
sections.head: Right way, wrong turn
sections.caption: the China model and COVID
body: For a while, Ajay Shah said, the China model seemed to work. Hundreds of mil­lions came out of poverty, and global cap­i­tal­ism, whose prac­ti­tion­ers “go along with a pre­vail­ing con­sen­sus”, com­mit­ted it­self to the China story.

Amit Varma re­called a scene from Richard McGregor’s *The Party*. In 2008, with the fi­nan­cial cri­sis just break­ing in America, Wang Qishan, the vice pre­mier in charge of fi­nance, told vis­it­ing American busi­ness­men: “You have your way. We have our way, our way is right.” {016-S04}
Then came Xi Jinping[[x10]], and with him, Shah said, “a huge step back to­wards Maoism”.
## The vac­cine no­body trusted

COVID ex­posed the cost. India made no pre­tence of build­ing its own vac­cine, Shah said: the Oxford-AstraZeneca shot came with help from the Gates Foundation and was made at giant scale by a pri­vate Indian com­pany. China, in­sist­ing it had ar­rived, pushed its own vac­cines, which pro­tected poorly. {016-S10}
Many older Chinese re­fused them. “So if the gov­ern­ment says this is a made in China vac­cine, you know some­thing is wrong,” Shah said. Plenty, he added, will not even drink made-in-China milk.

~ Varma added that the dis­trust is prac­ti­cal, not moral: au­thor­i­tar­ian gov­ern­ments face bad in­cen­tives and “will al­ways be in­com­pe­tent”. {016-C14} Each act of cru­elty, Shah replied, teaches a hun­dred friends and fam­ily that the regime can­not be trusted. {#bayes}

quote.text: When you’ve lived in an au­thor­i­tar­ian coun­try, you know the gov­ern­ment is an enemy and not a friend.

sections.label: The perfect storm
sections.head: Target practice
sections.caption: the perfect storm
body: Ajay Shah flagged an un­com­fort­able phrase used in China, one he said no free coun­try should use: macroe­co­nomic man­age­ment.

Officials pulled four levers, land, con­struc­tion, in­fra­struc­ture and credit, to hit a GDP tar­get year after year, and on paper China had con­quered the busi­ness cycle[[x12]]. “So when­ever there’s a GDP tar­get, you gotta get ner­vous that some­thing is not going right in this coun­try,” Shah said. {016-C10}
Infrastructure built to prop up growth could be a road to nowhere[[x11]]. A pri­vate de­vel­oper would not build one, Shah said, be­cause it wor­ries about get­ting paid. {016-C11}

Amit Varma, who ob­jects that GDP counts gov­ern­ment spend­ing, said of such growth: “it is a shadow, it is a chimera”. He added that their own show was a road to nowhere: “It’s a labour of love, no re­turns.”
## Never a bad year

Capitalism needs booms and busts to cre­ate the right in­cen­tives, Shah ar­gued. {016-C12} China’s pump-priming pro­duced 50-year-old busi­ness lead­ers who had never known a down­turn, and cap­i­tal went to who­ever bor­rowed most and cosied up to the party.
Then Xi Jinping turned the state on the other three elites, busi­ness, in­tel­lec­tual and cul­tural, and fam­i­lies sent their chil­dren and money abroad. {016-C13}
~ Nor was it wise to pick fights with the ad­vanced economies, Shah said, which make up 60 to 70 per cent of world GDP. {#worldgdp}

quote.text: A good in­fra­struc­ture project is one that earns some plau­si­ble re­turn on eq­uity.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the perfect storm

sections.label: Through the decades
sections.head: Pawns with minds of their own
sections.caption: the man of system
body: Amit Varma began his his­tory of mod­ern China with Mao, and with Adam Smith’s “man of sys­tem”[[x13]], who imag­ines he can ar­range a so­ci­ety like pieces on a chess­board. Friedrich Hayek called the same error the fatal con­ceit[[x14]]. {016-C07}

Deng Xiaoping changed much, but not the ma­chine. Reading from Richard McGregor’s *The Party*, Varma said the party kept its grip on per­son­nel, pro­pa­ganda and the army. One uni­ver­sity pro­fes­sor, quoted by McGregor, put it this way: “The party is like God. He is ev­ery­where. You just can’t see him.” {016-J14}
In place of ter­ror came what McGregor calls a take-it-or-leave-it com­pact: stay out of pol­i­tics, and you and your fam­ily can get on with your lives and maybe get rich. {016-C09}
## Two cars
Many did. In *Smoke and Mirrors*, Pallavi Aiyar recorded a stu­dent whose fa­ther had cy­cled miles to work and who now owned two cars. Everybody, she told Varma, said some ver­sion of it. {016-S08}
Did that end jus­tify the means? Not for Ajay Shah: state mur­der and cru­elty are be­yond the pale, and gains in in­come add less to hap­pi­ness than peo­ple as­sume. {016-C17}

~ Nor, he ar­gued, does co­er­cive growth last. Authoritarian rule breeds a cul­ture of obe­di­ence that kills ini­tia­tive and cre­ativ­ity, and the knowl­edge of how to be free can­not be switched on at will.

quote.text: In the great chess­board of human so­ci­ety, every sin­gle piece has a prin­ci­ple of mo­tion of its own
quote.who: Adam Smith, as read by Amit Varma

quote.text: As long as there is a cer­tain level of elite ca­pa­bil­ity, it can be the bridge and con­nect into glob­al­i­sa­tion. And then you’re off to the races.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A dotted line, a broken boy, a screaming app and caged songbirds

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on when the USSR looked like the future
stories.head: Samuelson’s dots never joined
body: The most im­por­tant eco­nom­ics text­book in world his­tory, Ajay Shah said, car­ried a prophecy on its in­side cover. In edi­tion after edi­tion, Paul Samuelson printed there a chart of the GDP of var­i­ous coun­tries.
“Samuelson al­ways had a dot dot dot line with pro­jec­tions for the fu­ture where he ex­pected that the USSR would beat the United States in terms of its ag­gre­gate GDP,” Shah said. {016-S02}

The faith had a his­tory. In 1905 Tsarist Russia lost a war to Japan. After the rev­o­lu­tion of 1917 came forced mod­erni­sa­tion: fac­to­ries, sci­ence, tech­nol­ogy and five-year plans, along with what Shah called “mind-boggling lev­els of cru­elty”. Millions were mur­dered.

By 1945 the Soviet Union had beaten Adolf Hitler, with a great deal of Western help, and was the great land power of the world[[x15]]. By 1949 it had a nu­clear bomb, built partly on ideas stolen from the Manhattan Project. {#bomb}
George Orwell, Arthur Koestler and Jawaharlal Nehru all re­jected the regime’s cru­elty. But many still be­lieved that, in a purely in­stru­men­tal way, the model was going to work.

It did not. The pro­jec­tion, Shah said, never came true. In 1989 the Soviet Union col­lapsed under the weight of its own con­tra­dic­tions, and the oc­cu­pied lands, fes­ter­ing with ha­tred and re­sent­ment, walked away the mo­ment they could.
~ Russia, Shah said, has never got its mojo back. “It’s a Spain sized GDP. Frankly, it’s just Saudi Arabia with nukes.” {016-J01}
stories.why: Even the best econ­o­mists can mis­take a co­er­cive sprint for a durable growth model. The case for un­free­dom, Shah ar­gued, failed on its own in­stru­men­tal terms, not only on eth­i­cal ones.
stories.postscript: When Shah likened Russia to Spain and Saudi Arabia, Amit Varma imag­ined lis­ten­ers from both coun­tries protest­ing, in Hindi, at being dragged in.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Samuelson’s dotted line

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the cruelty that shaped China’s reformer
stories.head: A son, a window, and term limits
body: During the Cultural Revolution, Ajay Shah said, Red Guards threw Deng Xiaoping’s son, then about 11 or 14 years old, out of a first-floor win­dow. The boy broke his bones and was crip­pled for life. {016-S05}
“So, in a way, Deng Xiaoping deeply knew the hor­ror of Chinese com­mu­nism,” Shah said. When Deng came to power in 1978[[x17]], he had no il­lu­sions about the regime.

He built guardrails. The head of state could serve only ten years, and a suc­ces­sion sys­tem was cre­ated where Mao and the Soviet Union had none. Abroad, Deng’s phrase was “we should bide our time”: China was weak, needed Western tech­nol­ogy and cap­i­tal, and should not pick fights. {016-J12}
~ Xi Jinping, Shah said, undid it all[[x16]]. He aban­doned the term lim­its and gath­ered power to him­self and his cronies. {#termlimits}
stories.why: The re­forms came from a man who had felt the regime’s cru­elty in his own fam­ily. That ex­plains why he spread power out, and why Xi gath­er­ing it back mat­ters so much.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Deng Xiaoping’s son

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on China’s lockdowns and the phone as jailer
stories.head: One street too far
body: China met COVID with some of the world’s most ex­treme lock­downs, Ajay Shah said, and with a tri­umphal­ism that the Chinese way was bet­ter. Month after month, peo­ple were trapped in their homes.

Mobile phones, dig­i­tal iden­tity and track­ing were turned against them. “People could not move into the next street be­cause the app would start scream­ing, and then a gov­ern­ment of­fi­cial would come after that per­son,” Shah said. {016-S11}
Factories stopped, flights stopped, and sup­ply chains around the world were dis­rupted. There were even protests on the streets, which Shah called very un­usual in China.
~ Far from a tri­umph, Shah said, China be­came the world’s worst COVID night­mare. In the end the regime gave up. COVID surged, and lots of peo­ple died. {#surge}

quote.text: the abil­ity of the mod­ern dig­i­tal rev­o­lu­tion to de­stroy the lives of in­di­vid­u­als when placed in the hands of an au­thor­i­tar­ian coun­try

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s lament for cultures under long tyranny
stories.head: Songbirds on the expressway
body: In Pallavi Aiyar’s *Smoke and Mirrors*, Beijing is a sur­real place. Old bent men in Mao suits walk their caged song­birds along an ex­press­way. {#songbirds} Elderly women prac­tise tai chi sur­rounded by bull­doz­ers.

What struck Aiyar most was “the lack of vis­i­ble trauma or re­sis­tance”. Amit Varma found that sad and wor­ry­ing. Part of him be­lieves bot­tom-up cul­ture al­ways out­lasts top-down rule; an­other part says cul­tural change can be driven by state co­er­cion, es­pe­cially the longer a regime lasts: as they say, par­a­digms change one fu­neral at a time.
Sometimes, he said, the op­pres­sive regime may win. {016-S09}

~ He saw that ten­sion in Lahore in 2006[[x19]], fol­low­ing the Indian cricket team as a jour­nal­ist. His fa­ther was born there but felt no nos­tal­gia for it. Varma found a warm, ef­fu­sive Punjabi cul­ture, and be­side it a dark­ness com­ing from the regime’s ide­ol­ogy.

quote.text: Sometimes in this clash be­tween an op­pres­sive regime and a lib­er­ated cul­ture, the op­pres­sive regime may win out.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 16. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Deng Xiaoping (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Xi Jinping (Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain); Four Pests Campaign (China Government, public domain); Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Alison Bechdel (20Nasium26, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: China’s Future
shelf.creator: David Shambaugh
shelf.why: His pick if you read just one book on China.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Essential Dykes To Watch Out For
shelf.creator: Alison Bechdel
shelf.why: The comic strip ran for roughly 1985 to 2008 and be­came iconic.

shelf.title: Fun Home
shelf.creator: Alison Bechdel
shelf.why: Amit calls her 2006 mem­oir a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: Blankets
shelf.creator: Craig Thompson
shelf.why: One of the graphic nov­els Amit calls a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: Ghost World
shelf.creator: Daniel Clowes
shelf.why: Another graphic novel Amit calls a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: The Party: The Secret World of China’s Communist Rulers
shelf.creator: Richard McGregor
shelf.why: He calls it a great book on how the party re­ally works.

shelf.title: Smoke And Mirrors
shelf.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
shelf.why: Amit calls Aiyar a fan­tas­tic writer and a sharp an­a­lyst, not just a travel writer.

shelf.title: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
shelf.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
shelf.why: Yuen Yuen Ang’s ac­count of what ac­tu­ally hap­pened in China, which backs Amit’s re­fusal to take a car­i­ca­tured, good-versus-evil view of a deeply com­plex coun­try.

shelf.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: Kuran’s the­ory of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and pref­er­ence cas­cades: regimes look unan­i­mously sup­ported until peo­ple dis­cover that oth­ers se­cretly dis­agree too.

shelf.title: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (Episode 349 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Timur Kuran
shelf.why: The long ver­sion of Timur Kuran’s ideas, from pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and the Soviet col­lapse to the long di­ver­gence.

shelf.title: The End of History?
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: Fukuyama’s essay cap­tures the post-1989 be­lief that lib­eral democ­racy had won the ar­gu­ment for good.

shelf.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: Smith’s often-overlooked philo­soph­i­cal mas­ter­piece, which coined the ‘man of system’, the plan­ner who treats peo­ple like chess pieces: the best warn­ing against Maoist-style grand de­signs.

shelf.title: The Fatal Conceit
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek names the core error be­hind cen­tral plan­ning and price con­trols: the be­lief that any­one can know enough to run a com­plex so­ci­ety from the top down, when the knowl­edge it needs is spread across ev­ery­one.

shelf.title: The Road to Serfdom
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s clas­sic ar­gu­ment for free­dom against state plan­ning: cen­tral plan­ning and its au­thor­i­tar­i­an­ism lead to serf­dom.

shelf.title: The Constitution of Liberty
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s case for free­dom, the book Margaret Thatcher used to de­clare her government’s creed.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit links Mao’s grand de­signs to de­mon­eti­sa­tion through one shared delu­sion, that a leader can re­design so­ci­ety to a mas­ter plan, and calls de­mon­eti­sa­tion the largest as­sault on prop­erty rights in human his­tory.

shelf.title: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and can­not mea­sure and how the num­ber is built, in­clud­ing how gov­ern­ment make-work and roads to nowhere in­flate it.

shelf.title: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on the eco­nom­ics and pol­i­tics of vac­cines, which Amit calls a pot­ted mas­ter­class on health­care: why pre­ven­tion beats cure, and why pub­lic health and health­care are dif­fer­ent things.

shelf.title: India’s Greatest Civil Servant (Episode 167 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Narayani Basu
shelf.why: Narayani Basu on V.P.

shelf.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Episode 11)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The show’s pro­duc­tiv­ity mantra: be­tween a great idea and its re­al­i­sa­tion lies drudgery, and the rem­edy is to keep doing the work until magic hap­pens.

laughs.text: Ajay on post-Soviet Russia: ‘It’s a Spain sized GDP. Frankly, it’s just Saudi Arabia with nukes.’ Amit imag­ines lis­ten­ers from Spain and Saudi Arabia protest­ing in Hindi: why drag us into this?

While Ajay is ex­plain­ing roads to nowhere, Amit: ‘we are pri­vate cap­i­tal­ists and Everything is Everything is like a road to nowhere. Where are the re­turns? We are just spend­ing on it. It’s a labor of love, no re­turns.’ Ajay: ‘we are so­cial­ists in our per­sonal life.’
After Ajay com­pares the thrill of a first bi­cy­cle with a first car, Amit: ‘Can I make a shame­ful con­fes­sion? I love my car, but I don’t know how to ride a cycle.’
Ajay sug­gests his own book, In Service of the Republic, for Deng Xiaoping. Amit: ‘That is the great­est plug I’ve ever seen some­body give for their own freak­ing book.’
On Shambaugh’s China’s Future, Amit: ‘I hadn’t heard of this book till 30 sec­onds ago, boss. If you had told me, I would have read it and taken notes and seemed more knowl­edge­able than I am.’
Amit: ‘you’re a card-carrying econ­o­mist as you have de­scribed your­self. I’ve never seen your card.’
Amit calls Hayek ‘one of our fa­vorite Freddies’. After the Thatcher story he adds: ‘So she had the same fa­vorite Freddie as I do.’
As Ajay de­scribes Xi stok­ing griev­ance, na­tion­al­ism and ha­tred of elites, Amit says drily: ‘I was think­ing all of this sounds fa­mil­iar, but carry on.’
How World War II was won, at­trib­uted by Ajay to ei­ther Churchill or Stalin: the Americans gave the trea­sure, the Russians gave the blood, and the British gave the time.
The party’s ver­dict on Mao, as Amit re­calls it from a 1981 party con­fer­ence: Mao was 70% right and 30% wrong, with his mer­its pri­mary and his er­rors sec­ondary.

A Chinese pro­fes­sor quoted by McGregor: ‘the party is like God. He is ev­ery­where. You just can’t see him.’ Law pro­fes­sor He Weifang adds that the party ‘is not even reg­is­tered as an organization’.

Before the 2007 Party Congress, Edict 19 of the pro­pa­ganda de­part­ment told ed­i­tors to strictly con­trol cov­er­age of the October Revolution an­niver­sary and ‘not play up the dis­in­te­gra­tion of the Soviet Union’.
Margaret Thatcher at her first cab­i­net meet­ing, slam­ming Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom on the table: ‘Gentlemen. This is what will guide us.’
Amit on how au­thor­i­tar­ian regimes re­shape cul­ture over time: ‘as they say par­a­digms change one fu­neral at a time.’
